questions.question: What is struct embedding in Go?
questions.title: Embedding Basics
questions.direct_answer: An unnamed field whose type name acts as the field name: type Admin struct { User; Level int }. The embedded type's fields and methods are PROMOTED — admin.Name and admin.Greet() work. Composition, not inheritance.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: An unnamed field whose type name acts as the field name: type Admin struct { User; Level int }. The embedded type's fields and methods are PROMOTED — admin.Name and admin.Greet() work. Composition, not inheritance.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
The mechanics under promotion, once more because it's the heart: name resolution is a depth-first walk. a.Level: found at depth 0 (Admin's own fields). a.Name: no depth-0 hit, descend into every embedded type (depth 1) — User has it — promoted. Shadowing: an outer Name at depth 0 wins before the walk descends. Ambiguity: TWO embedded types both providing Name at depth 1 — neither promotes (a.Name is a compile error); the explicit a.UserA.Name / a.UserB.Name resolves it.

The method promotion is a wrapper: a.Greet() compiles to the method-value equivalent of a.User.Greet() — receiver is the INNER struct. Two consequences: (1) the method's body sees the INNER's scope (its own promoted lookups resolve within User's chain, not Admin's — shadowing rules apply inside-out); (2) the method SET of Admin includes a Greet wrapper — which is what makes Admin satisfy Greeter — interface satisfaction composes through embedding, and that's the composition idiom's backbone.

Embedding an interface — the delegation pattern: type Handler struct { io.Reader } — Handler now HAS a Read method (promoted from the field), calls forward to whatever Reader was assigned to the field, AND Handler satisfies io.Reader. This is how wrappers get interface compliance for free: embed the interface you wrap, override only what you change, everything else forwards automatically. The standard library's shape everywhere: sort.Reverse embeds a sort.Interface and overrides Less — three lines that would be twenty in a hand-built wrapper.

The layout fact that surprises: the embedded field occupies real storage, exactly as a named field would (a.User is an actual User in Admin's memory). Embedding is purely a name-resolution + method-set convention laid over an ordinary field — which is why the SAME struct can embed AND name the same type: struct { User; other User } — two fields, one promoted path, one explicit. All the magic is lexical; none of it is structural.

questions.question: How does embedding differ from inheritance?
questions.title: When would you use Embedding Basics in a real project
questions.direct_answer: Embedding: has-a with promoted access; the inner stays itself (accessible via the field name); static binding; no subtype. Inheritance: is-a; virtual dispatch; the subtype IS the parent. Go chose composition — embedding — and interfaces for polymorphism, deliberately without the class hierarchy.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Embedding: has-a with promoted access; the inner stays itself (accessible via the field name); static binding; no subtype. Inheritance: is-a; virtual dispatch; the subtype IS the parent. Go chose composition — embedding — and interfaces for polymorphism, deliberately without the class hierarchy.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The comparison in terms that expose every difference:

1. Type relationship: inheritance makes Admin a User (assignable, substitutable — polymorphism through the hierarchy). Embedding makes Admin CONTAIN a User (a.User is a real field). No substitutability — code taking User cannot take Admin; there is no is-a.

2. Method binding: inheritance dispatches VIRTUALLY — child overrides reach the parent's call sites (fragile base: parent calls self.Method(), the child's override hijacks it). Embedding binds STATICALLY — Admin.Greet and User.Greet are separate; an outer shadow doesn't affect the inner's other methods, and calls to promoted methods always reach the embedded type's implementation.

3. Overriding: inheritance's override REPLACES. Embedding's outer shadow HIDES — the inner's method continues to exist and run wherever the inner type is used. Admin.Greet shadows; User.Greet is still what a User-typed variable calls, and still what a.User.Greet() gets.

4. Initialization and identity: an Admin must be constructed with a User IN it (Admin{User: ..., Level: 9}) — the composition is explicit at every creation site. Inheritance hides the parent's construction in the child's. The explicitness follows through equality, copying, JSON shape (the embedded User's fields FLATTEN into the outer's object — a serialization consequence, not a type-system one).

The design argument an interviewer wants articulated: inheritance bundles four things together — code reuse, subtyping, dynamic dispatch, and polymorphism — into one mechanism with known costs (fragile base, deep hierarchies, accidental coupling). Go splits the bundle: reuse → embedding; polymorphism + dispatch → interfaces. Each mechanism does one thing, and the type system stays decidable: method calls resolve statically except through interfaces, where the dispatch is explicit in the type (interface value). The cost is ceremony — where Java writes 'class Admin extends User implements Greeter,' Go writes an embedded field plus a method-set rule. The benefit is that every line of a Go program's behavior is traceable to a declaration in view.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The dependency comparison, mechanized: inheritance's override replaces — a child method substitutes for the parent's in ALL contexts, including calls the parent makes on itself (virtual dispatch reaching through the base). Embedding's shadow hides — the inner's method continues to exist and run wherever the inner type is used; only the unqualified outer path is shadowed. A parent calling its own Greet() still gets ITS Greet() in Go's model — there is no dispatch layer for the child's version to hijack — which is precisely the fragile-base-class failure mode Go designed out. The trade is explicitness: where inheritance gives you automatic specialization, Go requires you to write the outer method and route to the inner explicitly when you need both. That cost buys locality — every behavior question ('which Greet runs here?') is answerable from the types in view, never from a hierarchy walk.

The initialization story is the second axis: composition makes the inner explicit at construction (Admin{User: ...} — the Admin IS built from a User, visibly). Inheritance hides the parent's construction inside the child's — convenient until you need to know what was built. Go's literal syntax keeps the has-a honest: the memory layout is two adjacent values (or a pointer), and the promotion is name-resolution sugar over that layout — nothing more. Reviewers can read the embedding as what it physically is: a field with special lookup rules.

questions.question: Can you embed a pointer to a struct? What changes?
questions.title: a common mistake when using Embedding Basics
questions.direct_answer: Yes — type App struct { *User }. Promotion works the same for fields and methods (through the pointer). Differences: the embedded field is a POINTER (nil until set), method calls auto-deref through it, and the inner struct is SHARED — mutations through the embedder reach the original.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Yes — type App struct { *User }. Promotion works the same for fields and methods (through the pointer). Differences: the embedded field is a POINTER (nil until set), method calls auto-deref through it, and the inner struct is SHARED — mutations through the embedder reach the original.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Pointer embedding is legal and common:

```go
type App struct {
    *User        // embedded pointer
    Name  string
}

app := &App{User: &User{Name: "Al", Age: 30}, Name: "app"}
fmt.Println(app.Name2(), app.Greet())  // promotion through the pointer
```

Promotion is unchanged: fields (app.UserName via app.User.Name promoted to app.Name — through the pointer, auto-dereferenced like any pointer field access) and methods (app.Greet() → the embedded *User's method set, which per the superset rule includes User's value-receiver methods too).

What changes:

1. The embedded field is a pointer — nil until assigned. A zero App has app.User == nil — and promoted calls through it panic on the nil dereference. Zero-value usability is lost unless the methods are nil-safe; constructors become mandatory in practice.

2. Sharing: the pointee lives outside the App. Two Apps embedding the same *User share it — writes through one are visible through the other. With value embedding, each Admin has its own User copy.

3. Initialization: the literal must supply a *User — usually constructed inline (App{User: &User{...}}). The extra & is the visible sign of the indirection.

Where the shape earns its keep: shared-state composition (several handlers embedding a *Config — one config, live updates shared), and template patterns where the embedded pointer is assigned LATE (a framework sets it after construction — the struct is a shell until then). The standard library's sync package exhibits the value-embedding side (Mutex by value), while dependency-injection codebases lean on pointer embedding for shared services — both idioms, distinguished by who owns the lifetime.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The pointer-embed mechanics mirror pointer receivers: the promoted field access app.Name (through the embedded *User) compiles to an auto-dereference — (*app.User).Name — one indirection per access, same as any pointer field. The promoted method call app.Greet() routes through the *User's method set — which, by the superset rule, includes User's value-receiver methods too: everything a User can do, the pointer form can do.

The nil-embedded-pointer trap deserves the same prominence the typed-nil interface gets: a zero App has app.User == nil, and ANY promoted access panics on the nil dereference. Unlike the value-embed (zero Admin has a zero User — fields readable, methods callable), the pointer-embed's zero value is a landmine — which is why pointer-embedding types almost always ship with constructors that set the field. The pattern to recognize in review: type with a pointer-embed and NO NewX is asking for a nil-deref bug report.

The sharing semantics, mechanized: the embedded pointer field is one word in the struct — the pointee lives elsewhere. Copy the struct (assignment, value receiver): the pointer copies — both copies share the pointee. Two Apps embedding the same *User see each other's writes. Contrast value-embedding: each copy carries its own deep User. The choice is the classic value-vs-reference decision, moved to the field level — and the same rules (isolate vs share, immutable vs live) apply.

questions.question: How do embedded interfaces work — embedding an interface in a struct?
questions.title: compare Embedding Basics with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: Embedding io.Reader in a struct promotes the interface's METHODS: the struct satisfies io.Reader, and calls forward to the concrete value stored in the field. Delegation with compile-time checking — the wrapper idiom.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Embedding io.Reader in a struct promotes the interface's METHODS: the struct satisfies io.Reader, and calls forward to the concrete value stored in the field. Delegation with compile-time checking — the wrapper idiom.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Deep Dive
sections.content:
The forwarding wrapper, one layer down: the promoted Read on the struct is a compiler-generated method whose body is 'call l.Reader.Read' — a load of the embedded interface field (two words: itable + data) followed by the itable-dispatched call. The struct satisfies io.Reader without containing any Read code — satisfaction is the generated wrapper.

That indirection is what makes the decorator sound: your own Read shadows the promotion — your method runs; calling l.Reader.Read inside it reaches the ORIGINAL behavior. Every non-overridden method forwards the same way, so a wrapper embedding an interface and overriding one method is automatically correct for the rest — the compiler maintains the delegation, not hand-written forwarding methods.

The nil-embedded-interface edge: a zero wrapper has a nil interface field; promoted calls through it panic (nil interface method call). Constructors must set the field — the same mandatory-init pattern as pointer embedding, same cure.

What embedding an interface CANNOT do that concrete embedding can: promote FIELDS (interfaces have none) or grant the struct the concrete type's OTHER interfaces (promotion composes from the embedded type's method set — the interface's methods only). The two forms are complementary: concrete-in-struct for state+behavior, interface-in-struct for pure delegation; wrappers needing both embed both.

questions.question: What happens when two embedded types have a field or method with the same name?
questions.title: debug a problem involving Embedding Basics
questions.direct_answer: Ambiguity at that name: the outer reference x.Name is a compile error ('ambiguous selector'). The explicit paths resolve it: x.A.Name / x.B.Name. Shallower names shadow; same-depth ties need the full path.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Ambiguity at that name: the outer reference x.Name is a compile error ('ambiguous selector'). The explicit paths resolve it: x.A.Name / x.B.Name. Shallower names shadow; same-depth ties need the full path.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The conflict resolution rules, in order:

1. Depth wins: an outer type's own Name at depth 0 beats both embedded Names at depth 1 — the outer name SHADOWS, no ambiguity (access the inners via the explicit path).

2. Same depth is ambiguous: two embedded types both providing Name at depth 1 — x.Name doesn't compile:

```go
type A struct{ Name string }
type B struct{ Name string }
type C struct{ A; B }

c := C{A: A{"a"}, B: B{"b"}}
c.Name     // compile error: ambiguous selector
c.A.Name   // "a" — the resolution
c.B.Name   // "b"
```

3. Methods follow the same rules — two embedded types with Greet: c.Greet() ambiguous; c.A.Greet() explicit. And a method-vs-field tie at the same depth is also ambiguous (the selector can't choose).

The design choice: Go could have picked an order rule (first-embedded wins) — common in other composition systems — and rejected it: silent winner-picking breaks when someone reorders the embedded declarations (a refactor no reviewer would suspect). The ambiguity error makes the conflict VISIBLE at every use, forcing the explicit path — and the full path is self-documenting about which embedded type's member is meant.

The diamond case people ask about — A and B both embedding Base, then C embedding A and B: C sees Base's members at depth 2 through two paths. Same rule: any Base member referenced unqualified through C is ambiguous (two depth-2 routes); resolved via c.A.Base.X / c.B.Base.X. No diamond problem though — there's no shared SINGLE Base instance (the copies are independent — value embedding copies twice), and no virtual dispatch to disagree about. The ambiguity is lexical, the resolution is explicit, and the semantics (two separate Base sub-objects) are exactly what the memory layout says: embedding is fields, and fields don't unify.

The practical hygiene rule that falls out: keep embedded surfaces DISJOINT by design. Embed types with distinct field/method vocabularies (the(Logger) + the(Store) — no overlap, full promotion, zero ambiguity), and when overlap is real, prefer a named field for one of them — the ambiguity disappears entirely, because the name separates the surfaces.

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The ambiguity rule's mechanics: the selector resolution computes the set of candidate paths to the name at the SHALLOWEST depth where the name exists. One path — promoted. Two-plus paths at that depth — ambiguous — and the compiler reports it ('ambiguous selector'), refusing to pick. The design review that produced this: an order rule (first embedded wins) would be arbitrary-but-silent — reordering the embeds would change meaning with no error at any use site, the worst kind of breakage (semantic, invisible, version-controlled as 'just moved a field'). The ambiguity error makes every conflict explicit and forces the qualified name — which self-documents WHICH embedded type the member came from.

The diamond (A and B both embedding Base, C embedding A and B) follows the same rule — Base's members sit at depth 2 through two paths, so unqualified access is ambiguous, resolved via c.A.Base.X. But note what does NOT happen: no diamond PROBLEM — because there's no single shared Base to disagree about (value embedding copies twice — two independent Base sub-objects) and no dispatch to unify them. The ambiguity is lexical; the semantics are just two fields that happen to have the same type — which is what the memory says: embedding is fields, and fields don't unify.

The hygiene rule that prevents the whole class: embed types with disjoint surfaces (Logger + Store — no overlap, full promotion, zero ambiguity), and when real overlap exists, name one of the fields — the name separates the surfaces and the ambiguity vanishes before it can be discovered at a use site three files away.
